His saying: ﴿And they will know that Allah is the Manifest Truth﴾, meaning: His promise, His warning and His reckoning are the justice in which there is no injustice.

Commentary of Ibn Kathir (Tafsir al-Quran al-'Azim) on surah 24, verse 26:

Ibn 'Abbas said: "The wicked words are for wicked men, and wicked men are for wicked words. And the good words are for good men, and good men are for good words." He said: "It was revealed concerning 'Aishah and the people of the slander (ahl al-ifk)."

Likewise it has been narrated from Mujahid, 'Ata', Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Sha'bi, al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan al-Basri, Habib ibn Abi Thabit, and al-Dahhak. Ibn Jarir (al-Tabari) chose this view and justified it by saying that foul speech is more fitting for people of foulness among mankind, and good speech is more fitting for good people among mankind. Therefore, what the hypocrites attributed to 'Aishah, they are more deserving of it, and she is more deserving of innocence and purity than them. For this reason He said: ﴿Those are free from what they say﴾.

'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam said: "The wicked women are for wicked men, and wicked men are for wicked women, and the good women are for good men, and good men are for good women."

This also returns, by necessary implication, to what those earlier scholars said, meaning: Allah would not have made 'Aishah the wife of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) unless she were good, because he is the best of all good people among mankind. Had she been wicked, she would not have been suitable for him, neither by the Law nor by divine decree. For this reason He said: ﴿Those are free from what they say﴾, meaning they are far removed from what the people of falsehood and transgression say. ﴿For them is forgiveness﴾, meaning because of the lies that were said about them, ﴿and a noble provision﴾, meaning with Allah, in the Gardens of Bliss. In this there is a promise that the wife of the Prophet (ﷺ) will be in Paradise.

Ibn Abi Hatim said: Muhammad ibn Muslim narrated to us, Abu Nu'aym narrated to us, 'Abd al-Salam ibn Harb narrated to us, from Yazid ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, from al-Hakam, from Yahya ibn al-Jazzar, who said: Usayd ibn Jabir came to 'Abdullah and said: "I heard al-Walid ibn 'Uqbah speak a word that impressed me." 'Abdullah said: "Indeed, a believing man may have in his heart a word that is not good, which churns in his chest and does not settle until he utters it, and a man beside him hears it and takes it to himself. And indeed, a wicked man may have in his heart a good word which churns in his chest and does not settle until he utters it, and the man beside him hears it and takes it to himself." Then 'Abdullah recited: ﴿The wicked women are for wicked men, and the wicked men are for wicked women, and the good women are for good men, and the good men are for good women﴾.

Similar to this is what Imam Ahmad narrated in the Musnad, raised to the Prophet (ﷺ): "The likeness of one who hears wisdom and then does not relate except the evil of what he heard is like a man who came to a owner of sheep and said: 'Give me a sheep.' He said: 'Go and take by the ear whichever one you wish.' So he went and took hold of the ear of the sheep's dog." [Al-Musnad (2/353), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.] And in another hadith: "Wisdom is the lost property of the believer; wherever he finds it, he takes it." [Narrated by al-Tirmidhi in al-Sunan, no. (2687), and Ibn Majah in al-Sunan, no. (4169), through the route of 'Abdullah ibn Numayr, from Ibrahim ibn al-Fadl, from Sa'id al-Maqbari, from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him. al-Tirmidhi said: "This is a gharib hadith, which we only know from this route, and Ibrahim ibn al-Fadl al-Madani al-Makhzumi is weak in hadith due to his memory."]

These are the legal etiquettes (ādāb shar'iyyah) by which Allah disciplines His believing servants, and they concern seeking permission to enter (al-isti'dhān). Allah commanded the believers not to enter houses other than their own until they seek intimacy (yasta'nisū), meaning that they should ask permission before entering and greet after entering. It is recommended that one ask permission three times; if it is granted, well and good, and if not, one should leave. This is established in the Sahih, that Abu Musa asked permission from Umar three times, was not given permission, and left. Then Umar said: "Did I not hear the voice of Abdullah ibn Qays asking permission? Let him in." They searched for him and found that he had gone. When he came back afterwards, Umar said: "What made you return?" He said: "I asked permission three times and was not given permission, and I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'If one of you asks permission three times and is not given permission, let him leave.'" Umar said: "You must bring evidence for this, or I will beat you severely." So he went to a gathering of the Ansar and told them what Umar had said. They said: "None will testify for you except the youngest of us." So Abu Sa'id al-Khudri stood with him and informed Umar of that. Umar said: "The markets distracted me from it." [Sahih al-Bukhari, no. 6245, and Sahih Muslim, no. 2153.]

Imam Ahmad said: Abd al-Razzaq narrated to us, Ma'mar informed us, from Thabit, from Anas, or from someone else, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) asked permission to enter upon Sa'd ibn Ubadah and said: "As-salamu alaykum wa rahmatullah." Sa'd said: "Wa alaykum as-salam wa rahmatullah," but the Prophet (ﷺ) did not hear it until he had greeted three times, and Sa'd responded to him three times without the Prophet hearing it. The Prophet (ﷺ) turned back, and Sa'd followed him and said: "O Messenger of Allah, may my father and mother be your ransom, every greeting you gave was in my ear, and I responded to you but you did not hear me; I wanted to multiply your greetings and their blessing." Then he brought him into the house and offered him raisins, and the Prophet of Allah ate. When he finished he said: "The righteous have eaten your food, the angels have sent blessings upon you, and the fasting ones have broken their fast with you." [Al-Musnad, 3/138.]

Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i narrated, from the hadith of Abu Amr al-Awza'i: I heard Yahya ibn Abi Kathir say: Muhammad ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn Sa'd ibn Zurarah narrated to me, from Qays ibn Sa'd, who is the son of Ubadah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) visited us at our home and said: "As-salamu alaykum wa rahmatullah." Sa'd responded with a faint response. Qays said: I said: "Will you not permit the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to enter?" He said: "Leave him, he will increase the greetings upon us." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "As-salamu alaykum wa rahmatullah." Sa'd responded with a faint response. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "As-salamu alaykum wa rahmatullah." Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) turned back, and Sa'd followed him and said: "O Messenger of Allah, I was hearing your greeting, and I was responding to you with a faint response, so that you would increase the greetings upon us." He said: So he went away with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Sa'd ordered water for washing for him, and he washed, then he gave him a dyed cloak with saffron or waras, and he wrapped himself in it. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) raised his hands while saying: "O Allah, make Your blessings and mercy upon the family of Sa'd ibn Ubadah." He said: Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) partook of the food. When he wanted to leave, Sa'd brought him a donkey covered with a cloth, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) mounted it. Sa'd said: "O Qays, accompany the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." Qays said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Ride." I refused, so he said: "Either you ride, or you go away." He said: So I went away.

This has been narrated by another route [Sunan Abi Dawud, no. 5185, and al-Nasa'i in al-Sunan al-Kubra, no. 10157 and 10159, through Abdullah, from al-Awza'i, from Yahya ibn Abi Kathir, from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn Thawban, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to Sa'd ibn Ubadah as a visitor, and he mentioned the hadith]. It is a good and strong hadith, and Allah knows best.

Then it should be known that the one seeking permission to enter upon the people of a house should not stand directly facing the door, but should have the door to his right or left, because of what Abu Dawud narrated: Mu'ammal ibn al-Fadl al-Harrani narrated to us, along with others, who said: Baqiyyah narrated to us, Muhammad ibn Abd al-Rahman narrated to us, from Abdullah ibn Busr, who said: When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to the door of a people, he did not face the door directly, but from its right or left corner, and he would say: "As-salamu alaykum, as-salamu alaykum." That was because the houses did not have curtains over their doors at that time. Abu Dawud alone narrated it.

Abu Dawud also said: Uthman ibn Abi Shaybah narrated to us, Jarir narrated to us, (transition). Abu Dawud said: And Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shaybah narrated to us, Hafs narrated to us, from al-A'mash, from Talhah, from Hudhayl, who said: A man came, Uthman said: Sa'd, and stood at the door of the Prophet (ﷺ) seeking permission, and stood facing the door, Uthman said: facing the door. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "Move aside from it, or like this, for permission is [sought] to avoid looking." [Sunan Abi Dawud, no. 5174.]

Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi narrated it from Sufyan al-Thawri, from al-A'mash, from Talhah ibn Musarrif, from a man, from Sa'd, from the Prophet (ﷺ). Abu Dawud narrated it from his hadith. [Sunan Abi Dawud, no. 5175.]

In the two Sahihs, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "If a man had looked at you without permission, and you struck him with a pebble and blinded his eye, there would be no blame upon you." [Sahih al-Bukhari, no. 6902, and Sahih Muslim, no. 2158.]

The group [of compilers] narrated from the hadith of Shu'bah, from Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir, from Jabir, who said: I came to the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning a debt that my father had owed, and I knocked on the door. He said: "Who is it?" I said: "I." He said: "I, I," as if he disliked it. [Sahih al-Bukhari, no. 6250, Sahih Muslim, no. 2155, Sunan Abi Dawud, no. 5187, Sunan al-Tirmidhi, no. 2711, al-Nasa'i in al-Sunan al-Kubra, no. 10160, and Sunan Ibn Majah, no. 3709.]

He disliked that because this expression does not identify its speaker until he states his name or the kunyah by which he is known; otherwise everyone refers to himself as "I," and the purpose of seeking permission, which is the intimacy commanded in the verse, is not achieved by it.

Al-Awfi narrated from Ibn Abbas: "al-istinas" means "al-istidhan" (seeking permission). Many others said the same.

Ibn Jarir said: Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, Muhammad ibn Ja'far narrated to us, Shu'bah narrated to us, from Abu Bishr, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas regarding this verse: ﴿Do not enter houses other than your own until you seek intimacy and greet their people﴾ [he said]: It is only a scribal error: "until you seek permission and greet."

Hushaym narrated it likewise from Abu Bishr, who is Ja'far ibn Iyas. Mu'adh ibn Sulayman narrated from Ja'far ibn Iyas, from Sa'id, from Ibn Abbas, similarly, and added: Ibn Abbas used to recite: "until you seek permission and greet," and he used to recite according to the reading of Ubayy ibn Ka'b, may Allah be pleased with him.

This is very strange from Ibn Abbas.

Hushaym said: Mughirah informed us, from Ibrahim, who said: In the codex of Ibn Mas'ud: "until you greet its people and seek permission." This is also a narration from Ibn Abbas, and it is the choice of Ibn Jarir.

Imam Ahmad said: Rawh narrated to us, Ibn Jurayj narrated to us, Amr ibn Abi Sufyan informed me, that Amr ibn Abi Safwan informed him, that Kaladah ibn al-Hanbal informed him, that Safwan ibn Umayyah sent him during the Conquest with milk, young goat, and cucumbers, while the Prophet (ﷺ) was at the upper part of the valley. He said: I entered upon him without greeting and without seeking permission. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Go back and say: 'As-salamu alaykum, may I enter?'" That was after Safwan had embraced Islam. [Al-Musnad, 3/414.]

Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa'i narrated it from the hadith of Ibn Jurayj. Al-Tirmidhi said: Hasan gharib; we do not know it except from his hadith.

Abu Dawud said: Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shaybah narrated to us, Abu al-Ahwas narrated to us, from Mansur, from Ribi, who said: A man from the Banu Amir narrated to us, who sought permission from the Prophet (ﷺ) while he was in his house, and said: "May I enter?" The Prophet (ﷺ) said to his servant: "Go out to this man and teach him permission, and say to him: 'Say: As-salamu alaykum, may I enter?'" The man heard it and said: "As-salamu alaykum, may I enter?" The Prophet (ﷺ) permitted him, and he entered. [Sunan Abi Dawud, no. 5177.]

Hushaym said: Mansur informed us, from Ibn Sirin, and Yunus ibn Ubayd informed us, from Amr ibn Sa'id al-Thaqafi, that a man sought permission from the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "May I enter, or may we enter?" The Prophet (ﷺ) said to a female slave of his, called Rawdah: "Get up and teach him. He does not know how to seek permission properly. Tell him: say, 'As-salamu alaykum, may I enter?'" The man heard it, said it, and he said: "Enter." [Narrated by al-Tabari in his Tafsir, 18/87.]

Al-Tirmidhi said: al-Fadl ibn al-Sabah narrated to us, Sa'id ibn Zakariyya narrated to us, from Anbasah ibn Abd al-Rahman, from Muhammad ibn Zadhan, from Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir, from Jabir ibn Abdullah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Greeting precedes speech." [Sunan al-Tirmidhi, no. 2699.]

Then al-Tirmidhi said: Anbasah is weak in narration and abandoned; Muhammad ibn Zadhan is munkar al-hadith (his narrations are rejected).

Hushaym said: Mughirah said: Mujahid said: Ibn Umar came from a need, and the heat had afflicted him, so he came to the tent of a woman of Quraysh and said: "As-salamu alaykum, may I enter?" She said: "Enter in peace." He repeated, and she repeated, while he was shifting his weight between his feet. He said: "Say: 'Enter.'" She said: "Enter." So he entered. [Narrated by al-Tabari in his Tafsir, 18/87.]

Ibn Abi Hatim said: Abu Sa'id al-Ashajj narrated to us, Abu Nu'aym al-Ahwal narrated to us, Khalid ibn Iyas narrated to us, my grandmother Umm Iyas narrated to me, she said: I was with four women seeking permission [to enter upon A'ishah]. I said: "Shall we enter?" She said: "No. Let your companion say, 'Seek permission.'" She said: "As-salamu alaykum, may we enter?" She said: "Enter." Then she recited: ﴿O you who have believed, do not enter houses other than your own until you seek intimacy and greet their people﴾ [the verse].

Hushaym said: Ash'ath ibn Sawwar informed us, from Kurdus, from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: It is incumbent upon you to seek permission before your mothers and your sisters. Ash'ath said, from Adi ibn Thabit: A woman of the Ansar said: "O Messenger of Allah, I am in my house in a state that I do not like anyone to see me in, neither parent nor child, and a man of my family keeps entering upon me while I am in that state?" So this was revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, do not enter houses other than your own until you seek intimacy and greet their people﴾. [Narrated by al-Tabari in his Tafsir, 18/87.]

Ibn Juraij said: I heard 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah report from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "There are three verses which people have denied. Allah said: ﴿Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you﴾ [al-Hujurat: 13]. He said: And people say: 'The most noble of them in the sight of Allah is the one with the greatest house.'" He said: "And people have denied the whole matter of seeking permission (al-idhn)." He said: I said: "May I seek permission to enter upon my sisters, orphans in my care, who live with me in one house?" He said: "Yes." So I went back to him asking that he grant me a concession, but he refused. He said: "Would you like to see them naked?" I said: "No." He said: "Then seek permission." He said: I returned to him again, and he said: "Would you like to obey Allah?" I said: "Yes." He said: "Then seek permission."

Ibn Juraij said: Ibn Tawus reported to me from his father, who said: "There is no woman whose nakedness I would dislike more to see than that of a woman who is a mahram (unmarriageable kin)." He said: And he would be strict about this.

Ibn Juraij said, from al-Zuhri: I heard Hudhail ibn Shurahbil al-Awdi al-A'mha say that he heard Ibn Mas'ud say: "It is incumbent upon you to seek permission before entering upon your mothers."

Ibn Juraij said: I asked 'Ata': "Should a man seek permission before entering upon his wife?" He said: "No."

This is to be understood as indicating that it is not obligatory; otherwise, it is better that he inform her of his entry and not surprise her with it, since she may be in a state in which she does not wish him to see her.

Abu Ja'far ibn Jarir said: al-Qasim narrated to us, al-Husayn narrated to us, Muhammad ibn Hazim narrated to us, from al-A'mash, from 'Amr ibn Murrah, from Yahya ibn al-Jazzar, from the nephew of Zaynab, the wife of 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, from Zaynab, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: "When 'Abd Allah came back from a need and reached the door, he would clear his throat and spit, out of dislike that we should come upon something he disliked." (Tafsir al-Tabari 18/88.) Its chain is sound.

Ibn Abi Hatim said: Ahmad ibn Sinan al-Wasiti narrated to us, 'Abd Allah ibn Numayr narrated to us, al-A'mash narrated to us, from 'Amr ibn Murrah, from Abu Hubayra [in some copies: "Ubayda"], who said: "When 'Abd Allah entered the house, he would seek familiarity (istanasa), i.e., speak and raise his voice."

Mujahid said regarding ﴿until you seek familiarity﴾: "They clear their throats, or they cough."

It is related from Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal, may Allah have mercy on him, that he said: "When a man enters his house, it is recommended for him to clear his throat or to move his sandals."

For this reason, it has come in the Sahih, from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, that he forbade a man to come to his family suddenly at night (turuq), and in another narration: "at night, in a way that would betray them" (Sahih al-Bukhari, nos. 5243, 5244; Sahih Muslim, no. 715, from the hadith of Jabir, may Allah be pleased with him).

In another hadith: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ arrived at Madinah during the day, and he made his camel kneel outside it and said: "Wait until nightfall, that is, the end of the day, so that the disheveled woman may comb her hair and the woman whose husband is absent may shave her pubic hair" (narrated by al-Bukhari in his Sahih, no. 5247, from the hadith of Jabir, may Allah be pleased with him).

Ibn Abi Hatim said: My father narrated to us, Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shaybah narrated to us, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Sulayman narrated to us, from Wasil ibn al-Sa'ib, who said: Abu Sawra, the nephew of Abu Ayyub, narrated to me, from Abu Ayyub, who said: "I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, this is the greeting (salam), so what is the istinas?' He said: 'A man speaks with a glorification (tasbih), a takbir and a tahmid, and clears his throat, so that the people of the house are alerted.'" This is a strange hadith (gharib). (Narrated by Ibn Abi Shaybah in al-Musannaf (8/607), and from his route Ibn Majah in al-Sunan no. 3707, and al-Tabarani in al-Mu'jam al-Kabir (4/178), from 'Ubayd ibn Ghannam, from Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shaybah, with the same chain. Al-Busayri said in al-Zawa'id (3/171): "This chain is weak.")

Qatadah said regarding His saying ﴿until you seek familiarity﴾: "It is the seeking of permission." He said: It used to be said: "Seeking permission is three times. Whoever is not given permission in them should return. As for the first, it is so that the household may hear. As for the second, they should take their precaution. As for the third, if they wish they may grant permission, and if they wish they may refuse. Do not stand at the door of people who have turned you away from their door, for people have needs and occupations, and Allah is most entitled to excuse."

Muqatil ibn Hayyan said regarding His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, do not enter houses other than your own until you seek familiarity and greet their occupants﴾: "In the Jahiliyyah, when a man met his companion, he would not greet him, but would say: 'May you be greeted in the morning, and may you be greeted in the evening,' and this was the greeting of the people among themselves. One of them would go to his companion and would not seek permission, but would barge in and say: 'I have entered.' This would burden the man, and perhaps he would be with his family. So Allah changed all of that, to bring about concealment and chastity, and made it pure, clean, and free from filth, dirt and grime, and He said: ﴿O you who have believed, do not enter houses other than your own until you seek familiarity and greet their occupants﴾."

What Muqatil said is good. For this reason He said: ﴿That is better for you﴾, meaning: seeking permission is better for you, in the sense that it is better for both parties: for the one seeking permission and for the people of the house. ﴿That you may remember﴾.

* *

His saying: ﴿And if you do not find anyone in them, do not enter them until permission is given to you﴾. This is because of what it involves of disposing of another's property without his permission. If he wishes, he may permit; and if he wishes, he may not permit. ﴿And if you are told, "Go back," then go back; it is purer for you﴾, meaning: if they turn you away from the door, before permission or after it, ﴿then go back; it is purer for you﴾, meaning: your going back is purer for you and more proper. ﴿And Allah is Knowing of what you do.﴾

Qatadah said: Some of the Muhajirun said: "I have sought this verse my whole life and have not attained it: that I seek permission to enter upon one of my brothers, and he says to me, 'Go back,' and I go back while I am pleased [by his saying]: ﴿And if you are told, "Go back," then go back; it is purer for you, and Allah is Knowing of what you do.﴾"

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: ﴿And if you are told, "Go back," then go back﴾, meaning: do not stand at the doors of people.

* *

His saying: ﴿There is no blame upon you for entering uninhabited houses in which there is provision for you. And Allah knows what you reveal and what you conceal.﴾ This noble verse is more specific than the one before it, for it permits entering houses in which no one is present, without permission, when there is provision belonging to you in them, such as a house prepared for a guest, once permission has been given for it the first time, that suffices.

Ibn Juraij said: Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿Do not enter houses other than your own﴾, then it was abrogated and made an exception, saying: ﴿There is no blame upon you for entering uninhabited houses in which there is provision for you.﴾ The same is related from 'Ikrimah and al-Hasan al-Basri.

Others said: It refers to the houses of merchants, such as caravanserais (khanat), lodgings of travelers, the houses of Makkah, and others. Ibn Jarir chose this view and related it from a group of scholars. The first view is more apparent, and Allah knows best.

Malik said, from Zayd ibn Aslam: It refers to houses of hair (tents).

These are the legal etiquettes (ādāb shar'iyyah) by which Allah disciplines His believing servants, and they concern seeking permission to enter (al-isti'dhān). Allah commanded the believers not to enter houses other than their own until they seek intimacy (yasta'nisū), meaning that they should ask permission before entering and greet after entering. It is recommended that one ask permission three times; if it is granted, well and good, and if not, one should leave. This is established in the Sahih, that Abu Musa asked permission from Umar three times, was not given permission, and left. Then Umar said: "Did I not hear the voice of Abdullah ibn Qays asking permission? Let him in." They searched for him and found that he had gone. When he came back afterwards, Umar said: "What made you return?" He said: "I asked permission three times and was not given permission, and I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'If one of you asks permission three times and is not given permission, let him leave.'" Umar said: "You must bring evidence for this, or I will beat you severely." So he went to a gathering of the Ansar and told them what Umar had said. They said: "None will testify for you except the youngest of us." So Abu Sa'id al-Khudri stood with him and informed Umar of that. Umar said: "The markets distracted me from it." [Sahih al-Bukhari, no. 6245, and Sahih Muslim, no. 2153.]

Imam Ahmad said: Abd al-Razzaq narrated to us, Ma'mar informed us, from Thabit, from Anas, or from someone else, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) asked permission to enter upon Sa'd ibn Ubadah and said: "As-salamu alaykum wa rahmatullah." Sa'd said: "Wa alaykum as-salam wa rahmatullah," but the Prophet (ﷺ) did not hear it until he had greeted three times, and Sa'd responded to him three times without the Prophet hearing it. The Prophet (ﷺ) turned back, and Sa'd followed him and said: "O Messenger of Allah, may my father and mother be your ransom, every greeting you gave was in my ear, and I responded to you but you did not hear me; I wanted to multiply your greetings and their blessing." Then he brought him into the house and offered him raisins, and the Prophet of Allah ate. When he finished he said: "The righteous have eaten your food, the angels have sent blessings upon you, and the fasting ones have broken their fast with you." [Al-Musnad, 3/138.]

Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i narrated, from the hadith of Abu Amr al-Awza'i: I heard Yahya ibn Abi Kathir say: Muhammad ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn Sa'd ibn Zurarah narrated to me, from Qays ibn Sa'd, who is the son of Ubadah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) visited us at our home and said: "As-salamu alaykum wa rahmatullah." Sa'd responded with a faint response. Qays said: I said: "Will you not permit the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to enter?" He said: "Leave him, he will increase the greetings upon us." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "As-salamu alaykum wa rahmatullah." Sa'd responded with a faint response. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "As-salamu alaykum wa rahmatullah." Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) turned back, and Sa'd followed him and said: "O Messenger of Allah, I was hearing your greeting, and I was responding to you with a faint response, so that you would increase the greetings upon us." He said: So he went away with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Sa'd ordered water for washing for him, and he washed, then he gave him a dyed cloak with saffron or waras, and he wrapped himself in it. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) raised his hands while saying: "O Allah, make Your blessings and mercy upon the family of Sa'd ibn Ubadah." He said: Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) partook of the food. When he wanted to leave, Sa'd brought him a donkey covered with a cloth, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) mounted it. Sa'd said: "O Qays, accompany the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." Qays said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Ride." I refused, so he said: "Either you ride, or you go away." He said: So I went away.

This has been narrated by another route [Sunan Abi Dawud, no. 5185, and al-Nasa'i in al-Sunan al-Kubra, no. 10157 and 10159, through Abdullah, from al-Awza'i, from Yahya ibn Abi Kathir, from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn Thawban, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to Sa'd ibn Ubadah as a visitor, and he mentioned the hadith]. It is a good and strong hadith, and Allah knows best.

Then it should be known that the one seeking permission to enter upon the people of a house should not stand directly facing the door, but should have the door to his right or left, because of what Abu Dawud narrated: Mu'ammal ibn al-Fadl al-Harrani narrated to us, along with others, who said: Baqiyyah narrated to us, Muhammad ibn Abd al-Rahman narrated to us, from Abdullah ibn Busr, who said: When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to the door of a people, he did not face the door directly, but from its right or left corner, and he would say: "As-salamu alaykum, as-salamu alaykum." That was because the houses did not have curtains over their doors at that time. Abu Dawud alone narrated it.

Abu Dawud also said: Uthman ibn Abi Shaybah narrated to us, Jarir narrated to us, (transition). Abu Dawud said: And Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shaybah narrated to us, Hafs narrated to us, from al-A'mash, from Talhah, from Hudhayl, who said: A man came, Uthman said: Sa'd, and stood at the door of the Prophet (ﷺ) seeking permission, and stood facing the door, Uthman said: facing the door. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "Move aside from it, or like this, for permission is [sought] to avoid looking." [Sunan Abi Dawud, no. 5174.]

Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi narrated it from Sufyan al-Thawri, from al-A'mash, from Talhah ibn Musarrif, from a man, from Sa'd, from the Prophet (ﷺ). Abu Dawud narrated it from his hadith. [Sunan Abi Dawud, no. 5175.]

In the two Sahihs, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "If a man had looked at you without permission, and you struck him with a pebble and blinded his eye, there would be no blame upon you." [Sahih al-Bukhari, no. 6902, and Sahih Muslim, no. 2158.]

The group [of compilers] narrated from the hadith of Shu'bah, from Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir, from Jabir, who said: I came to the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning a debt that my father had owed, and I knocked on the door. He said: "Who is it?" I said: "I." He said: "I, I," as if he disliked it. [Sahih al-Bukhari, no. 6250, Sahih Muslim, no. 2155, Sunan Abi Dawud, no. 5187, Sunan al-Tirmidhi, no. 2711, al-Nasa'i in al-Sunan al-Kubra, no. 10160, and Sunan Ibn Majah, no. 3709.]

He disliked that because this expression does not identify its speaker until he states his name or the kunyah by which he is known; otherwise everyone refers to himself as "I," and the purpose of seeking permission, which is the intimacy commanded in the verse, is not achieved by it.

Al-Awfi narrated from Ibn Abbas: "al-istinas" means "al-istidhan" (seeking permission). Many others said the same.

Ibn Jarir said: Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, Muhammad ibn Ja'far narrated to us, Shu'bah narrated to us, from Abu Bishr, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas regarding this verse: ﴿Do not enter houses other than your own until you seek intimacy and greet their people﴾ [he said]: It is only a scribal error: "until you seek permission and greet."

Hushaym narrated it likewise from Abu Bishr, who is Ja'far ibn Iyas. Mu'adh ibn Sulayman narrated from Ja'far ibn Iyas, from Sa'id, from Ibn Abbas, similarly, and added: Ibn Abbas used to recite: "until you seek permission and greet," and he used to recite according to the reading of Ubayy ibn Ka'b, may Allah be pleased with him.

This is very strange from Ibn Abbas.

Hushaym said: Mughirah informed us, from Ibrahim, who said: In the codex of Ibn Mas'ud: "until you greet its people and seek permission." This is also a narration from Ibn Abbas, and it is the choice of Ibn Jarir.

Imam Ahmad said: Rawh narrated to us, Ibn Jurayj narrated to us, Amr ibn Abi Sufyan informed me, that Amr ibn Abi Safwan informed him, that Kaladah ibn al-Hanbal informed him, that Safwan ibn Umayyah sent him during the Conquest with milk, young goat, and cucumbers, while the Prophet (ﷺ) was at the upper part of the valley. He said: I entered upon him without greeting and without seeking permission. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Go back and say: 'As-salamu alaykum, may I enter?'" That was after Safwan had embraced Islam. [Al-Musnad, 3/414.]

Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa'i narrated it from the hadith of Ibn Jurayj. Al-Tirmidhi said: Hasan gharib; we do not know it except from his hadith.

Abu Dawud said: Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shaybah narrated to us, Abu al-Ahwas narrated to us, from Mansur, from Ribi, who said: A man from the Banu Amir narrated to us, who sought permission from the Prophet (ﷺ) while he was in his house, and said: "May I enter?" The Prophet (ﷺ) said to his servant: "Go out to this man and teach him permission, and say to him: 'Say: As-salamu alaykum, may I enter?'" The man heard it and said: "As-salamu alaykum, may I enter?" The Prophet (ﷺ) permitted him, and he entered. [Sunan Abi Dawud, no. 5177.]

Hushaym said: Mansur informed us, from Ibn Sirin, and Yunus ibn Ubayd informed us, from Amr ibn Sa'id al-Thaqafi, that a man sought permission from the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "May I enter, or may we enter?" The Prophet (ﷺ) said to a female slave of his, called Rawdah: "Get up and teach him. He does not know how to seek permission properly. Tell him: say, 'As-salamu alaykum, may I enter?'" The man heard it, said it, and he said: "Enter." [Narrated by al-Tabari in his Tafsir, 18/87.]

Al-Tirmidhi said: al-Fadl ibn al-Sabah narrated to us, Sa'id ibn Zakariyya narrated to us, from Anbasah ibn Abd al-Rahman, from Muhammad ibn Zadhan, from Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir, from Jabir ibn Abdullah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Greeting precedes speech." [Sunan al-Tirmidhi, no. 2699.]

Then al-Tirmidhi said: Anbasah is weak in narration and abandoned; Muhammad ibn Zadhan is munkar al-hadith (his narrations are rejected).

Hushaym said: Mughirah said: Mujahid said: Ibn Umar came from a need, and the heat had afflicted him, so he came to the tent of a woman of Quraysh and said: "As-salamu alaykum, may I enter?" She said: "Enter in peace." He repeated, and she repeated, while he was shifting his weight between his feet. He said: "Say: 'Enter.'" She said: "Enter." So he entered. [Narrated by al-Tabari in his Tafsir, 18/87.]

Ibn Abi Hatim said: Abu Sa'id al-Ashajj narrated to us, Abu Nu'aym al-Ahwal narrated to us, Khalid ibn Iyas narrated to us, my grandmother Umm Iyas narrated to me, she said: I was with four women seeking permission [to enter upon A'ishah]. I said: "Shall we enter?" She said: "No. Let your companion say, 'Seek permission.'" She said: "As-salamu alaykum, may we enter?" She said: "Enter." Then she recited: ﴿O you who have believed, do not enter houses other than your own until you seek intimacy and greet their people﴾ [the verse].

Hushaym said: Ash'ath ibn Sawwar informed us, from Kurdus, from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: It is incumbent upon you to seek permission before your mothers and your sisters. Ash'ath said, from Adi ibn Thabit: A woman of the Ansar said: "O Messenger of Allah, I am in my house in a state that I do not like anyone to see me in, neither parent nor child, and a man of my family keeps entering upon me while I am in that state?" So this was revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, do not enter houses other than your own until you seek intimacy and greet their people﴾. [Narrated by al-Tabari in his Tafsir, 18/87.]

Ibn Juraij said: I heard 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah report from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "There are three verses which people have denied. Allah said: ﴿Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you﴾ [al-Hujurat: 13]. He said: And people say: 'The most noble of them in the sight of Allah is the one with the greatest house.'" He said: "And people have denied the whole matter of seeking permission (al-idhn)." He said: I said: "May I seek permission to enter upon my sisters, orphans in my care, who live with me in one house?" He said: "Yes." So I went back to him asking that he grant me a concession, but he refused. He said: "Would you like to see them naked?" I said: "No." He said: "Then seek permission." He said: I returned to him again, and he said: "Would you like to obey Allah?" I said: "Yes." He said: "Then seek permission."

Ibn Juraij said: Ibn Tawus reported to me from his father, who said: "There is no woman whose nakedness I would dislike more to see than that of a woman who is a mahram (unmarriageable kin)." He said: And he would be strict about this.

Ibn Juraij said, from al-Zuhri: I heard Hudhail ibn Shurahbil al-Awdi al-A'mha say that he heard Ibn Mas'ud say: "It is incumbent upon you to seek permission before entering upon your mothers."

Ibn Juraij said: I asked 'Ata': "Should a man seek permission before entering upon his wife?" He said: "No."

This is to be understood as indicating that it is not obligatory; otherwise, it is better that he inform her of his entry and not surprise her with it, since she may be in a state in which she does not wish him to see her.

Abu Ja'far ibn Jarir said: al-Qasim narrated to us, al-Husayn narrated to us, Muhammad ibn Hazim narrated to us, from al-A'mash, from 'Amr ibn Murrah, from Yahya ibn al-Jazzar, from the nephew of Zaynab, the wife of 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, from Zaynab, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: "When 'Abd Allah came back from a need and reached the door, he would clear his throat and spit, out of dislike that we should come upon something he disliked." (Tafsir al-Tabari 18/88.) Its chain is sound.

Ibn Abi Hatim said: Ahmad ibn Sinan al-Wasiti narrated to us, 'Abd Allah ibn Numayr narrated to us, al-A'mash narrated to us, from 'Amr ibn Murrah, from Abu Hubayra [in some copies: "Ubayda"], who said: "When 'Abd Allah entered the house, he would seek familiarity (istanasa), i.e., speak and raise his voice."

Mujahid said regarding ﴿until you seek familiarity﴾: "They clear their throats, or they cough."

It is related from Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal, may Allah have mercy on him, that he said: "When a man enters his house, it is recommended for him to clear his throat or to move his sandals."

For this reason, it has come in the Sahih, from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, that he forbade a man to come to his family suddenly at night (turuq), and in another narration: "at night, in a way that would betray them" (Sahih al-Bukhari, nos. 5243, 5244; Sahih Muslim, no. 715, from the hadith of Jabir, may Allah be pleased with him).

In another hadith: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ arrived at Madinah during the day, and he made his camel kneel outside it and said: "Wait until nightfall, that is, the end of the day, so that the disheveled woman may comb her hair and the woman whose husband is absent may shave her pubic hair" (narrated by al-Bukhari in his Sahih, no. 5247, from the hadith of Jabir, may Allah be pleased with him).

Ibn Abi Hatim said: My father narrated to us, Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shaybah narrated to us, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Sulayman narrated to us, from Wasil ibn al-Sa'ib, who said: Abu Sawra, the nephew of Abu Ayyub, narrated to me, from Abu Ayyub, who said: "I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, this is the greeting (salam), so what is the istinas?' He said: 'A man speaks with a glorification (tasbih), a takbir and a tahmid, and clears his throat, so that the people of the house are alerted.'" This is a strange hadith (gharib). (Narrated by Ibn Abi Shaybah in al-Musannaf (8/607), and from his route Ibn Majah in al-Sunan no. 3707, and al-Tabarani in al-Mu'jam al-Kabir (4/178), from 'Ubayd ibn Ghannam, from Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shaybah, with the same chain. Al-Busayri said in al-Zawa'id (3/171): "This chain is weak.")

Qatadah said regarding His saying ﴿until you seek familiarity﴾: "It is the seeking of permission." He said: It used to be said: "Seeking permission is three times. Whoever is not given permission in them should return. As for the first, it is so that the household may hear. As for the second, they should take their precaution. As for the third, if they wish they may grant permission, and if they wish they may refuse. Do not stand at the door of people who have turned you away from their door, for people have needs and occupations, and Allah is most entitled to excuse."

Muqatil ibn Hayyan said regarding His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, do not enter houses other than your own until you seek familiarity and greet their occupants﴾: "In the Jahiliyyah, when a man met his companion, he would not greet him, but would say: 'May you be greeted in the morning, and may you be greeted in the evening,' and this was the greeting of the people among themselves. One of them would go to his companion and would not seek permission, but would barge in and say: 'I have entered.' This would burden the man, and perhaps he would be with his family. So Allah changed all of that, to bring about concealment and chastity, and made it pure, clean, and free from filth, dirt and grime, and He said: ﴿O you who have believed, do not enter houses other than your own until you seek familiarity and greet their occupants﴾."

What Muqatil said is good. For this reason He said: ﴿That is better for you﴾, meaning: seeking permission is better for you, in the sense that it is better for both parties: for the one seeking permission and for the people of the house. ﴿That you may remember﴾.

* *

His saying: ﴿And if you do not find anyone in them, do not enter them until permission is given to you﴾. This is because of what it involves of disposing of another's property without his permission. If he wishes, he may permit; and if he wishes, he may not permit. ﴿And if you are told, "Go back," then go back; it is purer for you﴾, meaning: if they turn you away from the door, before permission or after it, ﴿then go back; it is purer for you﴾, meaning: your going back is purer for you and more proper. ﴿And Allah is Knowing of what you do.﴾

Qatadah said: Some of the Muhajirun said: "I have sought this verse my whole life and have not attained it: that I seek permission to enter upon one of my brothers, and he says to me, 'Go back,' and I go back while I am pleased [by his saying]: ﴿And if you are told, "Go back," then go back; it is purer for you, and Allah is Knowing of what you do.﴾"

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: ﴿And if you are told, "Go back," then go back﴾, meaning: do not stand at the doors of people.

* *

His saying: ﴿There is no blame upon you for entering uninhabited houses in which there is provision for you. And Allah knows what you reveal and what you conceal.﴾ This noble verse is more specific than the one before it, for it permits entering houses in which no one is present, without permission, when there is provision belonging to you in them, such as a house prepared for a guest, once permission has been given for it the first time, that suffices.

Ibn Juraij said: Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿Do not enter houses other than your own﴾, then it was abrogated and made an exception, saying: ﴿There is no blame upon you for entering uninhabited houses in which there is provision for you.﴾ The same is related from 'Ikrimah and al-Hasan al-Basri.

Others said: It refers to the houses of merchants, such as caravanserais (khanat), lodgings of travelers, the houses of Makkah, and others. Ibn Jarir chose this view and related it from a group of scholars. The first view is more apparent, and Allah knows best.

Malik said, from Zayd ibn Aslam: It refers to houses of hair (tents).

These are the legal etiquettes (ādāb shar'iyyah) by which Allah disciplines His believing servants, and they concern seeking permission to enter (al-isti'dhān). Allah commanded the believers not to enter houses other than their own until they seek intimacy (yasta'nisū), meaning that they should ask permission before entering and greet after entering. It is recommended that one ask permission three times; if it is granted, well and good, and if not, one should leave. This is established in the Sahih, that Abu Musa asked permission from Umar three times, was not given permission, and left. Then Umar said: "Did I not hear the voice of Abdullah ibn Qays asking permission? Let him in." They searched for him and found that he had gone. When he came back afterwards, Umar said: "What made you return?" He said: "I asked permission three times and was not given permission, and I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'If one of you asks permission three times and is not given permission, let him leave.'" Umar said: "You must bring evidence for this, or I will beat you severely." So he went to a gathering of the Ansar and told them what Umar had said. They said: "None will testify for you except the youngest of us." So Abu Sa'id al-Khudri stood with him and informed Umar of that. Umar said: "The markets distracted me from it." [Sahih al-Bukhari, no. 6245, and Sahih Muslim, no. 2153.]

Imam Ahmad said: Abd al-Razzaq narrated to us, Ma'mar informed us, from Thabit, from Anas, or from someone else, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) asked permission to enter upon Sa'd ibn Ubadah and said: "As-salamu alaykum wa rahmatullah." Sa'd said: "Wa alaykum as-salam wa rahmatullah," but the Prophet (ﷺ) did not hear it until he had greeted three times, and Sa'd responded to him three times without the Prophet hearing it. The Prophet (ﷺ) turned back, and Sa'd followed him and said: "O Messenger of Allah, may my father and mother be your ransom, every greeting you gave was in my ear, and I responded to you but you did not hear me; I wanted to multiply your greetings and their blessing." Then he brought him into the house and offered him raisins, and the Prophet of Allah ate. When he finished he said: "The righteous have eaten your food, the angels have sent blessings upon you, and the fasting ones have broken their fast with you." [Al-Musnad, 3/138.]

Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i narrated, from the hadith of Abu Amr al-Awza'i: I heard Yahya ibn Abi Kathir say: Muhammad ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn Sa'd ibn Zurarah narrated to me, from Qays ibn Sa'd, who is the son of Ubadah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) visited us at our home and said: "As-salamu alaykum wa rahmatullah." Sa'd responded with a faint response. Qays said: I said: "Will you not permit the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to enter?" He said: "Leave him, he will increase the greetings upon us." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "As-salamu alaykum wa rahmatullah." Sa'd responded with a faint response. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "As-salamu alaykum wa rahmatullah." Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) turned back, and Sa'd followed him and said: "O Messenger of Allah, I was hearing your greeting, and I was responding to you with a faint response, so that you would increase the greetings upon us." He said: So he went away with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Sa'd ordered water for washing for him, and he washed, then he gave him a dyed cloak with saffron or waras, and he wrapped himself in it. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) raised his hands while saying: "O Allah, make Your blessings and mercy upon the family of Sa'd ibn Ubadah." He said: Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) partook of the food. When he wanted to leave, Sa'd brought him a donkey covered with a cloth, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) mounted it. Sa'd said: "O Qays, accompany the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." Qays said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Ride." I refused, so he said: "Either you ride, or you go away." He said: So I went away.

This has been narrated by another route [Sunan Abi Dawud, no. 5185, and al-Nasa'i in al-Sunan al-Kubra, no. 10157 and 10159, through Abdullah, from al-Awza'i, from Yahya ibn Abi Kathir, from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn Thawban, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to Sa'd ibn Ubadah as a visitor, and he mentioned the hadith]. It is a good and strong hadith, and Allah knows best.

Then it should be known that the one seeking permission to enter upon the people of a house should not stand directly facing the door, but should have the door to his right or left, because of what Abu Dawud narrated: Mu'ammal ibn al-Fadl al-Harrani narrated to us, along with others, who said: Baqiyyah narrated to us, Muhammad ibn Abd al-Rahman narrated to us, from Abdullah ibn Busr, who said: When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to the door of a people, he did not face the door directly, but from its right or left corner, and he would say: "As-salamu alaykum, as-salamu alaykum." That was because the houses did not have curtains over their doors at that time. Abu Dawud alone narrated it.

Abu Dawud also said: Uthman ibn Abi Shaybah narrated to us, Jarir narrated to us, (transition). Abu Dawud said: And Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shaybah narrated to us, Hafs narrated to us, from al-A'mash, from Talhah, from Hudhayl, who said: A man came, Uthman said: Sa'd, and stood at the door of the Prophet (ﷺ) seeking permission, and stood facing the door, Uthman said: facing the door. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "Move aside from it, or like this, for permission is [sought] to avoid looking." [Sunan Abi Dawud, no. 5174.]

Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi narrated it from Sufyan al-Thawri, from al-A'mash, from Talhah ibn Musarrif, from a man, from Sa'd, from the Prophet (ﷺ). Abu Dawud narrated it from his hadith. [Sunan Abi Dawud, no. 5175.]

In the two Sahihs, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "If a man had looked at you without permission, and you struck him with a pebble and blinded his eye, there would be no blame upon you." [Sahih al-Bukhari, no. 6902, and Sahih Muslim, no. 2158.]

The group [of compilers] narrated from the hadith of Shu'bah, from Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir, from Jabir, who said: I came to the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning a debt that my father had owed, and I knocked on the door. He said: "Who is it?" I said: "I." He said: "I, I," as if he disliked it. [Sahih al-Bukhari, no. 6250, Sahih Muslim, no. 2155, Sunan Abi Dawud, no. 5187, Sunan al-Tirmidhi, no. 2711, al-Nasa'i in al-Sunan al-Kubra, no. 10160, and Sunan Ibn Majah, no. 3709.]

He disliked that because this expression does not identify its speaker until he states his name or the kunyah by which he is known; otherwise everyone refers to himself as "I," and the purpose of seeking permission, which is the intimacy commanded in the verse, is not achieved by it.

Al-Awfi narrated from Ibn Abbas: "al-istinas" means "al-istidhan" (seeking permission). Many others said the same.

Ibn Jarir said: Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, Muhammad ibn Ja'far narrated to us, Shu'bah narrated to us, from Abu Bishr, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas regarding this verse: ﴿Do not enter houses other than your own until you seek intimacy and greet their people﴾ [he said]: It is only a scribal error: "until you seek permission and greet."

Hushaym narrated it likewise from Abu Bishr, who is Ja'far ibn Iyas. Mu'adh ibn Sulayman narrated from Ja'far ibn Iyas, from Sa'id, from Ibn Abbas, similarly, and added: Ibn Abbas used to recite: "until you seek permission and greet," and he used to recite according to the reading of Ubayy ibn Ka'b, may Allah be pleased with him.

This is very strange from Ibn Abbas.

Hushaym said: Mughirah informed us, from Ibrahim, who said: In the codex of Ibn Mas'ud: "until you greet its people and seek permission." This is also a narration from Ibn Abbas, and it is the choice of Ibn Jarir.

Imam Ahmad said: Rawh narrated to us, Ibn Jurayj narrated to us, Amr ibn Abi Sufyan informed me, that Amr ibn Abi Safwan informed him, that Kaladah ibn al-Hanbal informed him, that Safwan ibn Umayyah sent him during the Conquest with milk, young goat, and cucumbers, while the Prophet (ﷺ) was at the upper part of the valley. He said: I entered upon him without greeting and without seeking permission. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Go back and say: 'As-salamu alaykum, may I enter?'" That was after Safwan had embraced Islam. [Al-Musnad, 3/414.]

Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa'i narrated it from the hadith of Ibn Jurayj. Al-Tirmidhi said: Hasan gharib; we do not know it except from his hadith.

Abu Dawud said: Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shaybah narrated to us, Abu al-Ahwas narrated to us, from Mansur, from Ribi, who said: A man from the Banu Amir narrated to us, who sought permission from the Prophet (ﷺ) while he was in his house, and said: "May I enter?" The Prophet (ﷺ) said to his servant: "Go out to this man and teach him permission, and say to him: 'Say: As-salamu alaykum, may I enter?'" The man heard it and said: "As-salamu alaykum, may I enter?" The Prophet (ﷺ) permitted him, and he entered. [Sunan Abi Dawud, no. 5177.]

Hushaym said: Mansur informed us, from Ibn Sirin, and Yunus ibn Ubayd informed us, from Amr ibn Sa'id al-Thaqafi, that a man sought permission from the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "May I enter, or may we enter?" The Prophet (ﷺ) said to a female slave of his, called Rawdah: "Get up and teach him. He does not know how to seek permission properly. Tell him: say, 'As-salamu alaykum, may I enter?'" The man heard it, said it, and he said: "Enter." [Narrated by al-Tabari in his Tafsir, 18/87.]

Al-Tirmidhi said: al-Fadl ibn al-Sabah narrated to us, Sa'id ibn Zakariyya narrated to us, from Anbasah ibn Abd al-Rahman, from Muhammad ibn Zadhan, from Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir, from Jabir ibn Abdullah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Greeting precedes speech." [Sunan al-Tirmidhi, no. 2699.]

Then al-Tirmidhi said: Anbasah is weak in narration and abandoned; Muhammad ibn Zadhan is munkar al-hadith (his narrations are rejected).

Hushaym said: Mughirah said: Mujahid said: Ibn Umar came from a need, and the heat had afflicted him, so he came to the tent of a woman of Quraysh and said: "As-salamu alaykum, may I enter?" She said: "Enter in peace." He repeated, and she repeated, while he was shifting his weight between his feet. He said: "Say: 'Enter.'" She said: "Enter." So he entered. [Narrated by al-Tabari in his Tafsir, 18/87.]

Ibn Abi Hatim said: Abu Sa'id al-Ashajj narrated to us, Abu Nu'aym al-Ahwal narrated to us, Khalid ibn Iyas narrated to us, my grandmother Umm Iyas narrated to me, she said: I was with four women seeking permission [to enter upon A'ishah]. I said: "Shall we enter?" She said: "No. Let your companion say, 'Seek permission.'" She said: "As-salamu alaykum, may we enter?" She said: "Enter." Then she recited: ﴿O you who have believed, do not enter houses other than your own until you seek intimacy and greet their people﴾ [the verse].

Hushaym said: Ash'ath ibn Sawwar informed us, from Kurdus, from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: It is incumbent upon you to seek permission before your mothers and your sisters. Ash'ath said, from Adi ibn Thabit: A woman of the Ansar said: "O Messenger of Allah, I am in my house in a state that I do not like anyone to see me in, neither parent nor child, and a man of my family keeps entering upon me while I am in that state?" So this was revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, do not enter houses other than your own until you seek intimacy and greet their people﴾. [Narrated by al-Tabari in his Tafsir, 18/87.]

Ibn Juraij said: I heard 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah report from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "There are three verses which people have denied. Allah said: ﴿Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you﴾ [al-Hujurat: 13]. He said: And people say: 'The most noble of them in the sight of Allah is the one with the greatest house.'" He said: "And people have denied the whole matter of seeking permission (al-idhn)." He said: I said: "May I seek permission to enter upon my sisters, orphans in my care, who live with me in one house?" He said: "Yes." So I went back to him asking that he grant me a concession, but he refused. He said: "Would you like to see them naked?" I said: "No." He said: "Then seek permission." He said: I returned to him again, and he said: "Would you like to obey Allah?" I said: "Yes." He said: "Then seek permission."

Ibn Juraij said: Ibn Tawus reported to me from his father, who said: "There is no woman whose nakedness I would dislike more to see than that of a woman who is a mahram (unmarriageable kin)." He said: And he would be strict about this.

Ibn Juraij said, from al-Zuhri: I heard Hudhail ibn Shurahbil al-Awdi al-A'mha say that he heard Ibn Mas'ud say: "It is incumbent upon you to seek permission before entering upon your mothers."

Ibn Juraij said: I asked 'Ata': "Should a man seek permission before entering upon his wife?" He said: "No."

This is to be understood as indicating that it is not obligatory; otherwise, it is better that he inform her of his entry and not surprise her with it, since she may be in a state in which she does not wish him to see her.

Abu Ja'far ibn Jarir said: al-Qasim narrated to us, al-Husayn narrated to us, Muhammad ibn Hazim narrated to us, from al-A'mash, from 'Amr ibn Murrah, from Yahya ibn al-Jazzar, from the nephew of Zaynab, the wife of 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, from Zaynab, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: "When 'Abd Allah came back from a need and reached the door, he would clear his throat and spit, out of dislike that we should come upon something he disliked." (Tafsir al-Tabari 18/88.) Its chain is sound.

It is related from Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal, may Allah have mercy on him, that he said: "When a man enters his house, it is recommended for him to clear his throat or to move his sandals."

For this reason, it has come in the Sahih, from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, that he forbade a man to come to his family suddenly at night (turuq), and in another narration: "at night, in a way that would betray them" (Sahih al-Bukhari, nos. 5243, 5244; Sahih Muslim, no. 715, from the hadith of Jabir, may Allah be pleased with him).

In another hadith: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ arrived at Madinah during the day, and he made his camel kneel outside it and said: "Wait until nightfall, that is, the end of the day, so that the disheveled woman may comb her hair and the woman whose husband is absent may shave her pubic hair" (narrated by al-Bukhari in his Sahih, no. 5247, from the hadith of Jabir, may Allah be pleased with him).

Ibn Abi Hatim said: My father narrated to us, Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shaybah narrated to us, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Sulayman narrated to us, from Wasil ibn al-Sa'ib, who said: Abu Sawra, the nephew of Abu Ayyub, narrated to me, from Abu Ayyub, who said: "I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, this is the greeting (salam), so what is the istinas?' He said: 'A man speaks with a glorification (tasbih), a takbir and a tahmid, and clears his throat, so that the people of the house are alerted.'" This is a strange hadith (gharib). (Narrated by Ibn Abi Shaybah in al-Musannaf (8/607), and from his route Ibn Majah in al-Sunan no. 3707, and al-Tabarani in al-Mu'jam al-Kabir (4/178), from 'Ubayd ibn Ghannam, from Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shaybah, with the same chain. Al-Busayri said in al-Zawa'id (3/171): "This chain is weak.")

Whoever is not given permission in them should return. As for the first, it is so that the household may hear. As for the second, they should take their precaution. As for the third, if they wish they may grant permission, and if they wish they may refuse. Do not stand at the door of people who have turned you away from their door, for people have needs and occupations, and Allah is most entitled to excuse."

* *

His saying: ﴿And if you do not find anyone in them, do not enter them until permission is given to you﴾. This is because of what it involves of disposing of another's property without his permission. * *

His saying: ﴿There is no blame upon you for entering uninhabited houses in which there is provision for you. And Allah knows what you reveal and what you conceal.﴾ This noble verse is more specific than the one before it, for it permits entering houses in which no one is present, without permission, when there is provision belonging to you in them, such as a house prepared for a guest, once permission has been given for it the first time, that suffices.
